summary: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive web simulator that turns space education into a mission. Students create an astronaut profile, complete four scored training modules, resolve a pre-launch fault, and fly a simulated Moon mission in which every decision changes oxygen, power, risk and score. In-flight emergencies such as a solar radiation storm, signal loss and an oxygen pressure drop teach real spaceflight concepts, with a scientific explanation after each choice. After a powered lunar landing, students complete six surface-science challenges, explore a NASA Data Explorer built on EPIC, DONKI, NeoWS, APOD and the NASA Image and Video Library, and receive a mission report and a project-generated certificate. ASTRA, a Gemini-powered AI Mission Control, gives guidance based on live mission telemetry. The project aims to make STEM learning active and accessible, contributing to UN SDGs 4, 9 and 13.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive web simulator where students learn space science by making decisions inside a Moon mission. A student enrolls as a cadet, completes four scored training modules (Space Science, Astronaut Survival, Spacecraft Systems, Mission Decision Making), resolves a deliberate pre-launch sensor fault, and launches. During flight, emergencies such as a solar radiation storm, deep space network signal loss, a cabin oxygen pressure drop and a radiator thermal runaway require a decision. A deterministic scenario engine updates oxygen, power, fuel, pressure, temperature, communications, navigation, mission health and risk based on that choice. Correct decisions lower risk; wrong decisions raise it and unlock harder emergencies. The student then performs a powered lunar descent (lunar gravity 1.62 m/s2, safe touchdown under 3.0 m/s), completes six surface-science challenges at Shackleton Crater, explores NASA data, and receives a scored mission report and a project-generated certificate.

NASA DATA AND ASTRA

A NASA Data Explorer shows Earth imagery (DSCOVR EPIC), space weather (DONKI), near-Earth objects (NeoWS), Astronomy Picture of the Day, and Moon imagery (NASA Image and Video Library). Data is fetched server-side and each item is labeled LIVE NASA STREAM or VERIFIED ARCHIVE; if an API is unavailable, clearly labeled archive data is shown and is never presented as live. ASTRA, our AI Mission Control built on the Google Gemini API, receives the live mission state (telemetry, phase, active emergency), so it coaches the student about the exact situation in front of them. It also works as a science tutor and falls back to a built-in knowledge base if the AI service is offline.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Space education is often passive: textbooks, videos and quizzes. Here students experience consequences and always see a scientific explanation of why a choice was right or wrong. This builds understanding of orbits, life support, radiation, communications and decision-making under pressure, and aims to inspire interest in STEM and space careers. It contributes, through education and awareness, to UN SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) and SDG 13 (Climate Action, via Earth observation and space weather data). It runs in a browser with no installation, so it can be used in classrooms and at home.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of another space quiz, we built a consequence-driven simulation. Every number on the mission dashboard changes because of a student action, and an AI Mission Control that sees the mission state turns the chatbot into a part of the mission. Real NASA data sits inside the mission experience rather than on a separate page. The scenario engine is data-driven, so new missions (Mars, Solar Storm Survival, ISS, Asteroid) can be added without rewriting the app.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Lucide React, canvas-confetti. Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, Pydantic. AI: Google Gemini API through a server-side proxy. Data: NASA open APIs (APOD, EPIC, DONKI, NeoWS, Image and Video Library). Progress is saved in the browser (localStorage). Deployed on Vercel [and backend host].

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: no invented NASA data; simulated values are clearly separate from real NASA data.

- Resilience: if a NASA or AI service fails, the app shows labeled fallback content instead of breaking.

- Security: API keys stay on the backend and in environment variables, never in the browser.

- Accessibility: icons plus text for alerts (not color alone), keyboard navigation, readable contrast, responsive layout for phones, tablets and laptops.

- Honesty: the certificate and ranks are project-generated, not official NASA credentials.

- Ease of use: a 3-minute Judge Fast-Track mode, saved progress, and logout / switch astronaut for shared devices.

USE OF AI TOOLS

AI coding tools (Google Antigravity) helped generate and iterate on the code, and Claude (Anthropic) helped draft documentation and presentation text. ASTRA uses Google Gemini at runtime. All AI-assisted work was reviewed and directed by the team. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers are used.

This is an educational simulation and is not affiliated with NASA.
